title: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems

topics.title: Atmospheric pressure and its vertical variation

learn.hook: A sealed packet of chips puffs up when you drive up to Mussoorie. The air outside is pressing on it less.
points: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of a column of air contained in a unit area from mean sea level to the top of the atmosphere. It is expressed in millibars (mb).
The average atmospheric pressure at sea level is 1,013.2 mb. Due to gravity, the air at the surface is denser and so has higher pressure.
Pressure is measured with a mercury barometer or an aneroid barometer.
In the lower atmosphere, pressure decreases rapidly with height, by about 1 mb for each 10 m increase in elevation (not always at the same rate).

The vertical pressure gradient force is much larger than the horizontal one, but it is generally balanced by a nearly equal and opposite gravitational force. Hence we do not experience strong upward winds.

example.q: Pressure at sea level is 1,013 mb. Using a fall of about 1 mb per 10 m, estimate the pressure at a hill town 500 m above sea level.
steps: Pressure = 1,013 − 50 = 963 mb.

learn.reallife: Aircraft altimeters work like aneroid barometers, converting the drop in air pressure into a height reading.

topics.title: Isobars and horizontal distribution of pressure

learn.hook: A weather map full of tightly packed lines over the Bay of Bengal is a warning: a strong wind system is brewing.
points: Small differences in horizontal pressure are highly significant for wind direction and velocity.
Isobars are lines connecting places having equal pressure. To remove the effect of altitude, pressure at every station is reduced to sea level before comparison.
A low-pressure system is enclosed by one or more isobars with the lowest pressure at the centre; a high-pressure system has the highest pressure at the centre.
The pressure gradient is the rate of change of pressure with distance. It is strong (steep) where isobars are close together and weak (gentle) where isobars are far apart.
Map reading: on world maps of sea-level pressure in January and July, the pressure belts can be traced, and their shift between the two months is visible.

example.q: On a map, isobars over region A are 50 km apart and over region B 200 km apart, with the same pressure interval. Where will winds be stronger?
steps: Closer isobars mean a steeper pressure gradient.
A steeper pressure gradient produces stronger winds.
Region A has isobars closer together.
example.answer: Region A, because its closely spaced isobars show a steep pressure gradient.

learn.reallife: IMD's daily weather charts show isobars; closely spaced isobars around a depression in the Bay of Bengal mean strong winds and a warning for fishermen.

topics.title: World pressure belts and their seasonal shift

learn.hook: The earth wears belts of pressure, alternating low and high from the equator to the poles, and the whole set shifts north and south with the seasons.
points: Near the equator, sea-level pressure is low: the equatorial low (equatorial trough).
Along 30°N and 30°S lie high-pressure areas called the subtropical highs.
Further polewards, along 60°N and 60°S, are low-pressure belts called the subpolar lows. Near the poles the pressure is high: the polar highs.
These pressure belts are not permanent in position. They oscillate with the apparent movement of the sun: in the Northern Hemisphere they move southwards in winter and northwards in summer.

example.q: List the pressure belts you cross flying from the North Pole to the equator.
steps: Start at the pole: polar high.
Around 60°N: subpolar low.
Around 30°N: subtropical high.
At the equator: equatorial low.
example.answer: Polar high → subpolar low (60°N) → subtropical high (30°N) → equatorial low.

learn.reallife: The northward shift of the equatorial low in summer over north India helps pull the south-west monsoon winds into the subcontinent.

topics.title: Forces affecting winds: pressure gradient, friction and Coriolis

learn.hook: Why do cyclones never form right at the equator? Because one invisible force, the Coriolis force, is zero there.
points: Wind is air moving from high pressure to low pressure. Its velocity and direction depend on three forces: the pressure gradient force, the frictional force and the Coriolis force (gravity acts downwards).
Pressure gradient force: the rate of change of pressure with distance. It is strong where isobars are close and weak where they are apart; it acts perpendicular to the isobars.
Frictional force affects wind speed. It is greatest at the surface and its influence generally extends up to 1–3 km. Friction is minimal over the sea surface.

Coriolis force, named after the French physicist who described it in 1844, results from the earth's rotation. It deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. Deflection is more when wind velocity is high.

The Coriolis force is directly proportional to the angle of latitude: maximum at the poles and absent at the equator. At the equator, wind blows perpendicular to the isobars and a low pressure fills up instead of intensifying, which is why tropical cyclones do not form near the equator.

example.q: A wind blows from south to north in the Northern Hemisphere. Which way will the Coriolis force deflect it?
steps: In the Northern Hemisphere, deflection is to the right of the direction of motion.
Facing north, your right is east.
So the wind is deflected towards the east (becoming south-westerly).
example.answer: To the right, i.e., towards the east.

learn.reallife: The south-east trade winds crossing the equator into the Indian Ocean are deflected to the right and arrive in India as the south-west monsoon.

topics.title: Geostrophic wind, cyclonic and anticyclonic circulation

learn.hook: In the Northern Hemisphere, a cyclone spins anticlockwise. Cross the equator, and the same storm would spin clockwise.
points: Winds in the upper atmosphere, 2–3 km above the surface, are free from surface friction and are controlled by the pressure gradient and the Coriolis force.
When isobars are straight and there is no friction, the pressure gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis force and the wind blows parallel to the isobars. This is the geostrophic wind.
Wind circulation around a low is cyclonic circulation; around a high it is anticyclonic circulation.

Directions (NCERT table): around a low (cyclone), anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere; around a high (anticyclone), clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

Over low-pressure areas, air converges and rises; over high-pressure areas, air subsides from above and diverges at the surface. Rising air (also from eddies, convection, orographic uplift and fronts) is essential for clouds and precipitation.

example.q: A low-pressure system lies over Australia. In which direction do its winds circulate?
steps: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere.
Circulation around a low is cyclonic.
In the Southern Hemisphere, cyclonic circulation is clockwise.

learn.reallife: Satellite images of cyclones hitting Odisha always show an anticlockwise swirl, because the Bay of Bengal is in the Northern Hemisphere.

topics.title: General circulation: ITCZ and the three cells

learn.hook: The atmosphere runs like three giant conveyor belts in each hemisphere, carrying heat from the tropics towards the poles.
points: The pattern of planetary winds depends on: latitudinal variation of heating, emergence of pressure belts, migration of the belts with the sun's apparent path, distribution of continents and oceans, and the earth's rotation.

At the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), high insolation causes convection and low pressure. Winds from the tropics converge here; the air rises to the top of the troposphere (up to about 14 km) and moves polewards.

Hadley cell (tropics): the air accumulates and sinks at about 30°N and S, forming the subtropical high. Near the surface, air flows back towards the equator as the easterlies (trade winds), which converge at the ITCZ.
Ferrel cell (middle latitudes): sinking cold air from the poles and rising warm air from the subtropical high; at the surface the winds are the westerlies.

Polar cell: cold, dense air subsides near the poles and blows towards the middle latitudes as the polar easterlies. These three cells set the pattern of general circulation, and the transfer of heat from lower to higher latitudes maintains it.

example.q: Name the surface winds in each cell of the Northern Hemisphere, from the equator to the pole.
steps: Hadley cell (0°–30°N): easterlies, i.e., the north-east trade winds.
Ferrel cell (30°–60°N): westerlies.
Polar cell (60°–90°N): polar easterlies.

learn.reallife: In July, the ITCZ shifts north over the Ganga plain, part of the system that draws the monsoon into India.

topics.title: El Nino, ENSO and seasonal winds

learn.hook: Warm water appearing off the coast of Peru can mean a weak monsoon in India. The atmosphere and the oceans are deeply linked.
points: The general circulation affects the oceans: large-scale winds start large, slow ocean currents, and oceans in turn supply energy and water vapour to the air.

Warming and cooling of the Pacific Ocean is most important. Warm water of the central Pacific slowly drifts towards the South American coast and replaces the cool Peruvian current. This appearance of warm water off Peru is called El Nino.
El Nino is closely linked with pressure changes in the Central Pacific and Australia; this change in pressure over the Pacific is the Southern Oscillation. The combined phenomenon is ENSO.
In strong ENSO years, the arid west coast of South America gets heavy rain, Australia faces drought (sometimes India too), and China faces floods. ENSO is monitored for long-range forecasting.

Seasonal winds: wind circulation is modified in different seasons by the shift of regions of maximum heating, pressure and wind belts. The most pronounced effect is the monsoon, especially over South-east Asia.

example.q: Why does IMD watch Pacific Ocean temperatures before forecasting India's monsoon?
steps: Warm water off Peru (El Nino) is linked with pressure changes over the Pacific (Southern Oscillation).
Strong ENSO causes large-scale weather variations around the world.
These can include drought in Australia and sometimes in India.
So ENSO helps in long-range monsoon forecasting.
example.answer: Because El Nino/ENSO can weaken India's monsoon, so it is used for long-range forecasting.

learn.reallife: IMD's long-range monsoon forecast each April mentions whether El Nino or La Nina conditions are expected in the Pacific.

topics.title: Local winds: land and sea breezes, mountain and valley winds

learn.hook: On Marina Beach in Chennai, the afternoon sea breeze brings relief. At night, the wind quietly reverses and blows out to sea.
points: Land and sea absorb and transfer heat differently. By day, land heats faster than the sea, so air over land rises and pressure falls, while the cooler sea has relatively high pressure. Wind blows from sea to land: the sea breeze.
At night the reverse happens: land loses heat faster and becomes cooler than the sea, so the pressure gradient is from land to sea, giving a land breeze.

Mountain and valley winds: by day, slopes heat up and air moves upslope, and air from the valley blows up the valley: the valley breeze. At night, slopes cool and dense air descends into the valley as the mountain wind.
Cool air from high plateaus and ice fields draining into valleys is called katabatic wind.

Warm winds occur on the leeward side of mountain ranges: moisture condenses and precipitates on the windward side; the dry air descending the leeward slope is warmed adiabatically and can melt snow quickly. Examples include the Foehn in the Alps and the Chinook in the Rockies.

example.q: At 3 p.m. on a sunny day in Mumbai, which way does the local wind blow? At 3 a.m.?
steps: 3 p.m.: land is warmer than the sea, so low pressure over land.
Wind blows from sea to land → sea breeze.
3 a.m.: land is cooler than the sea, so higher pressure over land.
Wind blows from land to sea → land breeze.
example.answer: 3 p.m.: sea breeze (sea to land); 3 a.m.: land breeze (land to sea).

topics.title: Air masses and their source regions

learn.hook: A cold wave that sweeps into north India in January carries the 'personality' of the frozen lands where its air was born.
points: When air stays over a homogeneous area (a vast ocean or plain) long enough, it acquires the characteristics of that area. Air with distinctive temperature and humidity is an air mass: a large body of air with little horizontal variation in temperature and moisture.
The homogeneous surfaces over which air masses form are their source regions. Air masses are classified by source region.

Five major source regions: (i) warm tropical and subtropical oceans; (ii) subtropical hot deserts; (iii) relatively cold high-latitude oceans; (iv) very cold snow-covered continents in high latitudes; (v) permanently ice-covered continents in the Arctic and Antarctica.
Types: maritime tropical (mT), continental tropical (cT), maritime polar (mP), continental polar (cP) and continental arctic (cA).
Tropical air masses are warm; polar air masses are cold. Maritime ones are moist; continental ones are dry.

example.q: Classify an air mass formed over the hot Sahara desert.
steps: Over land → continental (c).
Hot subtropical desert → tropical (T).
So it is continental tropical (cT): warm and dry.

learn.reallife: Moist maritime tropical air from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal feeds India's monsoon, while dry continental air dominates its winter.

teach.nudge: Define an air mass, name the source regions and the five types.

learn.hook: When a cold air mass charges into warm air, it acts like a snowplough, shoving the warm air up into towering clouds.
points: When two different air masses meet, the boundary zone between them is called a front. The process of formation of fronts is frontogenesis.
There are four types of fronts: cold, warm, stationary and occluded.
When cold air moves towards a warm air mass, the contact zone is a cold front. When warm air moves towards a cold air mass, the contact zone is a warm front.

When the front remains stationary, it is a stationary front. When an air mass is fully lifted above the land surface, it is an occluded front (this happens when a faster cold front overtakes a warm front).
Fronts occur in middle latitudes and are marked by steep gradients of temperature and pressure. They bring abrupt changes in temperature and cause air to rise, forming clouds and precipitation.

example.q: Name the front: (a) a cold air mass pushing into warm air; (b) a boundary that does not move for days; (c) warm air completely lifted off the ground by a cold front catching up.
steps: (a) Cold air advancing → cold front.
(b) Not moving → stationary front.
(c) Warm air fully lifted off the surface → occluded front.
example.answer: (a) Cold front; (b) Stationary front; (c) Occluded front.

learn.reallife: Western disturbances that bring winter rain and snow to north-west India are mid-latitude systems with frontal characteristics, originating over the Mediterranean region.

learn.hook: Most of Europe's rainy, windy weather comes from cyclones born where cold polar air meets warmer air: no warm ocean required.
points: Systems developing in mid and high latitudes, beyond the tropics, are called middle-latitude or extra-tropical cyclones. They form along the polar front.

Initially the front is stationary. In the Northern Hemisphere, warm air blows from the south and cold air from the north of the front. When pressure drops along the front, warm air moves north and cold air south, setting up an anticlockwise cyclonic circulation with a warm front and a cold front.

A warm sector is wedged between the forward and rear cold air. Warm air glides over the cold air ahead of the warm front, bringing a sequence of clouds and precipitation; behind, the cold front pushes the warm air up, forming cumulus clouds.
The cold front moves faster and overtakes the warm front. The warm air is completely lifted, the front is occluded, and the cyclone dissipates.

Differences from tropical cyclones: extra-tropical cyclones have a clear frontal system, cover a larger area, can originate over land and sea, and move from west to east; tropical cyclones have no fronts, originate only over seas and dissipate on land, have much higher wind velocity and are more destructive, and move from east to west.

example.q: Arrange the life cycle of an extra-tropical cyclone.
steps: A stationary polar front separates cold and warm air.
Pressure drops; warm air moves poleward and cold air equatorward; cyclonic circulation starts.
A warm front and a cold front develop with a warm sector between.
The faster cold front overtakes the warm front.
The warm air is lifted completely (occlusion) and the cyclone dies.
example.answer: Stationary front → wave and circulation → warm and cold fronts with warm sector → cold front overtakes → occlusion and dissipation.

learn.reallife: Western disturbances that bring snow to Kashmir and Himachal and winter rain to Punjab are linked with mid-latitude systems moving from west to east.

learn.hook: Cyclone Fani in 2019 struck Odisha with ferocious winds, yet timely evacuation of over a million people saved countless lives. Knowing how cyclones work saves lives.
points: Tropical cyclones are violent storms that originate over tropical oceans and move to coastal areas, causing destruction through violent winds, very heavy rain and storm surges. They are called cyclones in the Indian Ocean, hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the western Pacific and South China Sea, and willy-willies in western Australia.

Favourable conditions: (i) large sea surface with temperature higher than 27°C; (ii) presence of the Coriolis force; (iii) small variations in vertical wind speed; (iv) a pre-existing weak low-pressure area or low-level cyclonic circulation; (v) upper divergence above the sea-level system.

Energy comes from condensation in towering cumulonimbus clouds around the centre; a continuous supply of moisture from the sea strengthens the storm. On reaching land, the moisture supply is cut off and the storm dissipates. The place where it crosses the coast is the landfall.

Structure: the eye is a calm centre with subsiding air. Around it, the eye wall has strong spiralling ascent of air up to the tropopause, maximum winds (up to about 250 km/h) and torrential rain. Rain bands radiate outwards. The strongly circulating core around the eye can be 150–250 km across.

The whole storm system over the Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean is larger, about 600–1,200 km across, and it moves slowly, about 300–500 km per day. Cyclones crossing 20°N generally recurve and are more destructive. Storm surges inundate coastal lowlands.

example.q: A cyclone moves at 400 km per day. How long will it take to reach a coast 1,000 km away?
steps: Time = distance ÷ speed.
= 2.5 days.

learn.reallife: IMD's cyclone warnings and Odisha's network of cyclone shelters have made India a global example in reducing deaths from tropical cyclones.

learn.hook: In April and May, Kolkata often gets sudden evening storms called Kalbaisakhi: towering clouds, lightning and hail, all from one giant cumulonimbus.
points: Thunderstorms and tornadoes are severe local storms: of short duration and over a small area, but violent.

Thunderstorms are caused by intense convection on moist, hot days. A thunderstorm is a well-grown cumulonimbus cloud producing thunder and lightning. When clouds extend to heights with sub-zero temperature, hail forms and falls as a hailstorm. With insufficient moisture, a thunderstorm can generate dust storms.
A thunderstorm has an intense updraft of rising warm air that makes clouds grow taller, causing precipitation; later a downdraft brings cool air and rain to the ground.

From severe thunderstorms, a spiralling wind sometimes descends like an elephant's trunk with great force and very low pressure at the centre, causing massive destruction. This is a tornado. Tornadoes generally occur in middle latitudes; over the sea they are called water spouts.
These violent storms are the atmosphere's way of adjusting to uneven energy distribution: potential and heat energy are converted into kinetic energy, and the atmosphere returns to a stable state.

example.q: Why are thunderstorms more common on hot, humid afternoons?
steps: Strong heating makes air rise rapidly (intense convection).
Moist air cools as it rises and water vapour condenses.
Condensation releases heat, fuelling a towering cumulonimbus.
The cloud produces thunder, lightning and heavy rain.
example.answer: Because intense convection of moist, hot air builds cumulonimbus clouds by afternoon.

learn.reallife: IMD issues 'nowcasts' warning of thunderstorms and lightning a few hours ahead, and the Damini app alerts people about nearby lightning strikes.
